questions.question:
Consider the following functions, where [latex]n[/latex] is a positive integer.

[latex] n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)} [/latex]

Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?
Note: Assume the base of log to be [latex]2[/latex].
questions.explanation:
Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]):

- [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial.
- [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself.
- [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex].
- [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]).

So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex].

Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!)

questions.question:
Assume that the algorithms considered here sort the input sequences in ascending order. If the input is already in ascending order, which of the following are TRUE?
I. Quicksort runs in [latex]\Theta (n^{2})[/latex] time
II. Bubblesort runs in [latex]\Theta (n^{2})[/latex] time
III. Merge sort runs in [latex]\Theta (n)[/latex] time
IV. Insertion sort runs in [latex]\Theta (n)[/latex] time
questions.explanation:
On already sorted input:
- Quicksort (first/last element as pivot) makes the most unbalanced splits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n^2)[/latex] True
- Bubble sort with the "no swap" check stops after one pass [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] False
- Merge sort is always [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] False
- Insertion sort compares each element once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] True

Answer: I and IV only

questions.question:
A Young tableau is a 2D array of integers increasing from left to right and from top to bottom. Any unfilled entries are marked with [latex]\infty[/latex], and hence there cannot be any entry to the right of, or below a [latex]\infty[/latex]. The following Young tableau consists of unique entries.

When an element is removed from a Young tableau, other elements should be moved into its place so that the resulting table is still a Young tableau (unfilled entries may be filled in with a [latex]\infty[/latex]). The minimum number of entries (other than 1) to be shifted, to remove 1 from the given Young tableau is _______.
questions.explanation:
Removing 1 leaves a hole. Repeatedly fill it with the smaller of its right and lower neighbour:

- hole (1,1): min(2, 3) = 2 moves left
- hole (1,2): min(5, 4) = 4 moves up
- hole (2,2): min(6, 12) = 6 moves left
- hole (2,3): min(23, 18) = 18 moves up
- hole (3,3): min(25, [latex]\infty[/latex]) = 25 moves left
- hole (3,4) gets [latex]\infty[/latex]

Shifted: 2, 4, 6, 18, 25 = 5 entries

Answer: 5

questions.question: Suppose a polynomial time algorithm is discovered that correctly computes the largest clique in a given graph. In this scenario, which one of the following represents the correct Venn diagram of the complexity classes P, NP and NP Complete (NPC)?

Let [latex]f(n)=n[/latex] and [latex]g(n)=n^{1+sin \; n}[/latex] where n is a positive integer. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

[latex]g(n)=n^{1+\sin n}[/latex], and 1 + sin n keeps swinging between about 0 and 2. So g(n) is sometimes near 1 (much smaller than n) and sometimes near [latex]n^2[/latex] (much larger).
